On a regular grid, nearest-point is easy by rounding in any number of dimensions, so as written the claim 'easy in two dimensions, infeasible in hundreds' is wrong. The hardness lies in the grid being described by long, skewed directions; the private key is a short, nearly square description that makes it easy. That is also the missing forward and trapdoor direction.

The private key is a short, nearly square set of directions for the same grid, which makes the search easy for its holder'.

problem: TLS 1.3 also signs with RSA-PSS. RFC 8446 §4.2.3 makes rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 mandatory to implement, and most web servers still present RSA certificates. The chapter says so itself in the Fig 14.11 strip ('Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS'), the Fig 14.8 strip and ch14-publickey-p6. Read as written, the parenthesis tells the reader RSA plays no part in TLS 1.3.

RFC 8446 makes rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 mandatory to implement, most server certificates are RSA, and the chapter itself says 'Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS' (Fig 14.11 strip) and 'RSA ... only signs' (Fig 14.8 strip, ch14-publickey-p6). quote: was settled soon after in the Bernstein and Junger appeals, and it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source
problem: Neither case 'settled' the point. The Ninth Circuit withdrew the 1999 Bernstein panel opinion when it ordered an en banc rehearing, and in 2003 the case was dismissed without a ruling (Wikipedia, Bernstein v. United States). Only Junger v. Daley (6th Cir., 2000) still holds that source code is speech, and only in that circuit. Crypto libraries can be distributed openly today because of the January 2000 export rule (License Exception TSU for publicly available source code), not because of a settled ruling.
fix: "...that source code is protected speech, was upheld by appeals courts in the Bernstein (1999) and Junger (2000) cases, and together with the 2000 export rules it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source and globally distributed."
reason: Real. The 1999 Ninth Circuit Bernstein panel opinion was withdrawn when en banc rehearing was granted, and the case was dismissed in 2003 with no ruling. Only Junger v. Daley (6th Cir., 2000) holds that source code is protected speech, and only in that circuit. 'Settled' is wrong, and the export-rule change the paragraph has just described is the other half of why open crypto libraries are possible.
judge_fix: In ch14-history-p4 replace 'was settled soon after in the Bernstein and Junger appeals, and it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source and globally distributed' with: "was upheld on appeal in Junger v. Daley (2000), and together with those export rules it is why every cryptographic library today can be open source and globally distributed".

quote: several orders of magnitude beyond the entire computational capacity of Earth running until the heat death of the universe
problem: The arithmetic does not hold. 2^256 is about 1.2×10^77. Heat death is usually put at about 10^100 years (about 3×10^107 s), so even 10^21 operations per second for that long gives about 3×10^128 operations, far more than 2^256. The claim is true for the age of the universe: 4.4×10^17 s × about 10^22 ops/s ≈ 10^40, so 2^256 is about 37 orders of magnitude beyond. Also, the sentence follows 'an elliptic-curve key needs 256', but breaking a 256-bit curve key costs only about 2^128.
fix: "Trying every 256-bit key would take every computer on Earth far longer than the age of the universe." (This also matches ch14-primer-p3.)
reason: Real. 2^256 is about 1.2e77. Even at 1e21 to 1e22 operations a second, heat-death timescales (1e100 years) give about 1e128 or more operations, so the sentence is false as written. It holds against the age of the universe (about 37 orders of magnitude). 'Several orders' also undersells it. It also sits next to the elliptic-curve 256, which costs only about 2^128.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence of ch14-primer-p6 with: "A 256-bit symmetric key is out of reach: trying every key would take every computer on Earth far longer than the age of the universe." This matches ch14-primer-p3.

fix: "in the same performance class as RSA (well under a millisecond per operation on a modern server)"

quote: so that a certificate authority's (CA's) log of issued certificates can be publicly audited
problem: CT logs do not belong to the CA. They are independent public logs, run by operators such as Google and Cloudflare, and they accept certificates from every CA. That independence is what lets them catch a misbehaving CA, which ch14-tls-pqc-p4 describes correctly.
fix: "uses Merkle trees so that the public logs of every certificate the certificate authorities (CAs) issue can be audited without downloading every certificate."
reason: Real. Certificate Transparency logs (RFC 6962) are independent public logs that accept certificates from every CA. They are not a CA's own log, and that independence is what makes them catch a bad CA. ch14-tls-pqc-p4 describes it correctly, so the two places disagree.
judge_fix: ch14-hashing-p4, last sentence: "*Certificate Transparency* (Section 06 below) uses Merkle trees so that the public logs of every certificate the certificate authorities (CAs) issue can be audited without downloading every certificate."

quote: The hour after 11 o'clock is not 12; it is 0.
problem: On a real 12-hour clock the hour after 11 is 12, so the sentence states something false about clocks before it makes the modular point. A careful reader stops on it.
fix: "On a clock the hour after 11 wraps back to the top, 12, which arithmetic modulo 12 writes as 0."
reason: Real, though small. On an actual clock the hour after 11 is 12, so 'is not 12' is false of clocks before the modular point is made. The reader trips on it.

Cryptography does the same arithmetic, with the same algebraic properties (addition, multiplication, exponentiation), on a far larger clock: _5 + 9 mod 12 = 2_ is exactly the operation it performs, with a 2048-bit prime as the modulus instead of 12."

Even at today's roughly 10^21 operations per second, Earth's total over that time comes to about 10^128 operations, far more than 2^256 ≈ 10^77. Also, the callout's own example, a 256-bit elliptic-curve key, falls to about 2^128 work (the generic square-root attack), not 2^256.
reason: Duplicate of finding 4: the heat-death arithmetic does not hold (about 1e128 operations against 2^256 of about 1e77). The age of the universe is the defensible bound.

problem: ch14-hashing-p4: 'a certificate authority's (CA's) log of issued certificates'. problem: ch14-ecc-p4: 'Bitcoin's curve was picked for constants chosen by a simple public rule' states Satoshi's motive as fact. At 256 bits of key, ..."

quote: SLH-DSA rests only on the hash functions of Section 02.

Neither basis is factoring or discrete log, and no polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for either. SLH-DSA is the conservative hedge: if lattices turn out to hide a weakness, a signature that needs nothing but a hash function still stands."

ML-KEM and ML-DSA instead rest on lattice problems: a lattice is a regular grid of points extended to hundreds of dimensions, and finding the grid point nearest to a given point is easy in two dimensions and believed infeasible in hundreds, even for a quantum computer. SLH-DSA is the conservative hedge: if lattices turn out to hide a weakness, a signature that needs nothing but a hash function still stands." Rest of the paragraph (cost sentence) unchanged.
